extras.title: Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and settlement
extras.note: Several kingdoms formed amid migration, conflict and interaction with existing British communities; this was never one united state spanning the full frame.

extras.title: Rus’ principalities · regional realms
extras.note: An overlapping network of principalities, not a state created at one partition. Their later histories fed into several countries and cannot be assigned exclusively to modern Russia, Ukraine or Belarus.

extras.title: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
extras.note: A multiethnic polity that incorporated many western and southern Rus’ lands. It entered dynastic union with Poland and later the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; this map selects its relationship with Rus’, not its entire history.

maps.title: Aegean networks, Greek worlds & modern independence

connections.label: Bronze Age trade networks
connections.summary: Aegean communities exchanged objects, materials and diplomatic gifts with Egypt and West Asian courts.
connections.note: The Aegean entry is a regional cultural frame, not a united empire or the origin of Egyptian civilization.

connections.label: Crete–mainland exchange
connections.summary: Minoan Cretan art and exchange strongly influenced emerging Mycenaean court cultures.
connections.note: Interaction did not mean that all Minoans became Mycenaeans or that either label describes one state.

connections.label: Palace collapse & local change
connections.summary: The disintegration of Mycenaean palace systems was followed by regional early Iron Age societies.
connections.note: A gradual and uneven archaeological transition; people and practices persisted and no single invasion is asserted as its cause.

connections.label: Cities, writing & wider trade
connections.summary: City-states, alphabetic writing and wider overseas networks developed during the Geometric and early Archaic centuries.
connections.note: The period labels overlap in scholarly usage; this is cultural and institutional change, not a succession between two kingdoms.

connections.label: Archaic → Classical convention
connections.summary: The Persian Wars mark the conventional transition from Archaic to Classical Greek periodisation.
connections.note: Greek city-states remained politically distinct and neither period boundary marks the origin or disappearance of Greek people.

connections.label: Persian–Greek wars
connections.summary: Achaemenid campaigns and Greek resistance reshaped relations among Persian rulers and Greek city-states.
connections.note: The node groups many city-states, which pursued different alliances; this was not a war between two modern nation-states.

connections.label: Macedonian predominance
connections.summary: Macedonian royal power under Philip II provided the military and political base for Alexander’s conquests.
connections.note: Macedonia was one kingdom in the wider Greek world; the arrow does not turn every Greek city into a direct predecessor of his empire.

connections.label: Successor kingdoms emerge
connections.summary: Wars among Alexander’s successors produced multiple Hellenistic kingdoms and leagues.
connections.note: Hellenistic kingdoms is an umbrella period; it includes several dynasties and independent city alliances, not a single successor empire.

connections.label: Roman expansion in Greek East
connections.summary: Rome progressively defeated or annexed Hellenistic powers, with Ptolemaic Egypt annexed in 30 BC.
connections.note: Different states fell at different dates; Hellenistic cultures and artistic production continued under Roman government.

connections.label: War & independence recognition
connections.summary: The Greek war of independence led to international recognition of an independent Greek state in 1830 and subsequent settlement in 1832.
connections.note: The initial state comprised only part of present-day Greece; earlier Byzantine and ancient Greek histories were not one continuous sovereign state.

maps.title: Iron Age communities, Rome & post-Roman Britain

connections.label: Central European material networks
connections.summary: Hallstatt-period communities participated in the changing Iron Age networks represented by the wider central European frame.
connections.note: Hallstatt is an archaeological label; it cannot be equated with every Celtic or Germanic-speaking population or with a single ethnic homeland.

connections.label: Noricum enters Roman rule
connections.summary: The Norican kingdom was incorporated into Roman rule around 15 BC.
connections.note: The transition was largely peaceful in the museum account; formal provincial administration developed later, and this did not erase local communities.

connections.label: Rhine–Danube frontier exchange
connections.summary: Roman goods, diplomacy and military encounters connected imperial provinces with communities beyond the Rhine and Danube.
connections.note: Some regions were conquered and others remained outside Roman control; the arrow does not annex every society in the broad cultural frame.

connections.label: Claudius invades Britain
connections.summary: Roman armies invaded in 43 AD and progressively conquered much of present-day England and Wales.
connections.note: Conquest involved local allies and resistance and did not encompass the whole island; Iron Age communities did not disappear in 43.

connections.label: Resistance & Roman expansion
connections.summary: Roman expansion into western Iberia met prolonged resistance before imperial control consolidated.
connections.note: The cultural block’s 139 BC endpoint follows Viriathus’ death, not the end of Lusitanian communities or the completion of conquest.

connections.label: Long conquest of Hispania
connections.summary: Roman expansion gradually incorporated Iberian and Celtiberian communities across many separate campaigns.
connections.note: The last campaigns occurred under Augustus after the Republic’s conventional endpoint; languages, settlements and identities did not abruptly vanish.

connections.label: Carthaginian possessions lost
connections.summary: Rome displaced Carthaginian power in Iberia during the Second Punic War.
connections.note: The struggle did not immediately bring the entire peninsula under Roman control or end Indigenous resistance.

connections.label: Alésia & Roman conquest
connections.summary: Caesar’s victory over Vercingetorix and his allies at Alésia was a major stage in the conquest of Gaul.
connections.note: This is a selected campaign episode, not the disappearance of Gallic people or an instant conquest of every region.

connections.label: Rome among Italian communities
connections.summary: Early Rome developed within the culturally and linguistically diverse Italian peninsula.
connections.note: Italic peoples is a collective label including Latins; it does not include every early Italian culture, and Rome was not their united kingdom.

connections.label: Monarchy → republic
connections.summary: Roman tradition dates the replacement of royal rule by republican government to 509 BC.
connections.note: Early Roman chronology combines archaeology and much later literary accounts; 753 BC is a traditional foundation date, not a securely documented founding event.

connections.label: Augustan principate
connections.summary: Augustus’ settlement marks the conventional transition to imperial government within the Roman state.
connections.note: The western timeline entry overlaps the shared Roman Empire frame used in other maps; it is not a separate state founded alongside it in 27 BC.

connections.label: Roman government ends in Britain
connections.summary: Central Roman government in Britain ended and local authorities and kingdoms developed.
connections.note: The empire continued elsewhere; Sub-Roman Britain is a regional frame, not a new united British kingdom or a total population replacement.

connections.label: Settlement, conflict & coexistence
connections.summary: Migrants from continental northern Europe and existing British communities interacted as several Anglo-Saxon kingdoms formed.
connections.note: This overlaps the Sub-Roman frame, includes conflict and coexistence, and does not describe the whole island becoming Anglo-Saxon.

connections.label: English kingdom consolidates
connections.summary: Kings of Wessex and their successors consolidated territories into a kingdom of England during the tenth century.
connections.note: A protracted process involving Mercian, Northumbrian, Scandinavian and other territories, rather than a voluntary merger of all Britain; British kingdoms continued elsewhere.

connections.label: Suevic kingdom in former provinces
connections.summary: Suevic rulers established a kingdom in northwestern Iberian lands formerly under Roman authority.
connections.note: Changing rule over a selected region, not succession to the whole Roman Empire or disappearance of its provincial population.

connections.label: Suevic realm incorporated
connections.summary: Visigothic rule incorporated the Suevic kingdom in 585.
connections.note: This ended a separate government, not its population or all local religious institutions.

connections.label: Umayyad conquest
connections.summary: Arab and Berber armies defeated Visigothic royal forces and conquered most of Iberia.
connections.note: Al-Andalus includes many later governments, while northern Christian realms and frontier zones followed different histories.

connections.label: Northern frontier kingdoms
connections.summary: The Asturian monarchy developed in the north while Umayyad rulers governed much of Iberia.
connections.note: A frontier relationship with warfare, settlement and exchange; Asturias was not a complete successor to al-Andalus or all Visigothic territory.

connections.label: Royal centre moves to León
connections.summary: The royal centre shifted from Oviedo to León and the monarchy became known as the kingdom of León.
connections.note: Asturian and Leonese labels overlap; this was a change of political centre within a developing monarchy, not replacement of one people by another.

connections.label: Portucale within northern expansion
connections.summary: The recovery of Porto formed the setting for the first Portucalense county under the northern Christian monarchy.
connections.note: A regional county within changing royal authority; its exact endpoints vary, and it was not an independent kingdom of Portugal.

connections.label: County reconstituted
connections.summary: A new Portucalense county was assigned to Henry of Burgundy in 1096.
connections.note: Nuno Mendes’s defeat in 1071 ended the first comital line. Royal administration and later reorganisation preceded Henry’s county; these entries do not indicate an unbroken independent state.

connections.label: Afonso adopts kingship
connections.summary: Afonso Henriques adopted royal status after 1139, followed by Leonese recognition in 1143 and papal recognition in 1179.
connections.note: Kingship, recognition and territorial consolidation were separate stages; the kingdom’s borders and institutions continued to change.

connections.label: Castile–León dynastic union
connections.summary: Ferdinand III united the crowns of Castile and León in 1230.
connections.note: León retained a recognised royal identity within the composite crown; dynastic union did not instantly homogenise its institutions or population.

connections.label: Granada surrendered
connections.summary: Ferdinand and Isabella’s forces took Granada, the last Muslim-ruled Iberian kingdom, in 1492.
connections.note: This ended the Nasrid government, not Muslim people or culture; conversion, persecution, expulsions and continuing communities belong to later histories.

connections.label: Movement into Roman territories
connections.summary: Germanic-speaking groups were among the many populations that migrated, fought and settled within and beyond the Roman frontier.
connections.note: Migration Period is a broad historical frame, not a tribe or successor state; it also involves Huns, Slavs and others.

connections.label: Frankish kings consolidate Gaul
connections.summary: Clovis and later Frankish rulers consolidated kingdoms in former Roman Gaul.
connections.note: The Franks were one set of Germanic-speaking groups; the broad cultural label did not turn into a single Frankish nation.

connections.label: Post-imperial Alpine authorities
connections.summary: The end of western imperial rule left changing authorities in the eastern Alpine provinces.
connections.note: The selected regional frame includes Ostrogothic influence and local continuity; it was never one kingdom called Alpine kingdoms.

connections.label: Bavarian dukes attested
connections.summary: Agilolfing dukes are attested in the Bavarian region during the sixth century.
connections.note: Bavarian political formation was gradual; no secure single founding event or direct succession from every post-Roman Alpine authority is asserted.

connections.label: Tassilo deposed
connections.summary: Charlemagne deposed Duke Tassilo III and incorporated Bavaria under direct Carolingian authority.
connections.note: Bavaria remained a recognisable region and later duchy; the act did not end Bavarian communities.

connections.label: Charlemagne crowned emperor
connections.summary: Charlemagne received the imperial title in Rome in 800 while ruling the Frankish realm.
connections.note: The imperial-period block overlaps the broader Frankish entry; Carolingian kingship began earlier and the coronation did not absorb the Byzantine Empire.

connections.label: Babenberg frontier appointment
connections.summary: The emperor assigned the eastern march to Liutpold of the Babenberg family in 976.
connections.note: The march was a subordinate frontier jurisdiction associated with Bavaria, not an independent state replacing the empire.

connections.label: Austria raised to a duchy
connections.summary: The Privilegium minus raised Austria to a duchy and separated its ducal authority from Bavaria.
connections.note: It remained within the Holy Roman Empire; this was a legal and dynastic change rather than the birth of the modern republic.

connections.label: Archducal privileges confirmed
connections.summary: Emperor Frederick III confirmed privileges that recognised the Austrian archducal title.
connections.note: The claims originated in Rudolf IV’s fourteenth-century forgery; the Habsburg dynasty had already ruled Austria since the late thirteenth century.

connections.label: Austrian imperial title created
connections.summary: Francis adopted the hereditary title Emperor of Austria over the Habsburg lands in 1804.
connections.note: The new empire overlapped the Holy Roman Empire until the latter’s dissolution in 1806; its constituent lands were not all identical with the Austrian archduchy.

connections.label: Eastern Roman reconquest
connections.summary: Justinian’s armies defeated the Ostrogothic kingdom through a prolonged war in Italy.
connections.note: Campaign endpoints differ by definition; reconquest damaged the peninsula and did not produce lasting control of all Italy.

connections.label: Lombard invasion
connections.summary: Lombards conquered substantial parts of Italy while the Eastern Romans retained other territories.
connections.note: Italy remained divided; this was not a complete transfer of Byzantine Italy or a conquest of the Byzantine Empire.

connections.label: Charlemagne takes Lombard crown
connections.summary: Charlemagne conquered the northern Lombard kingdom and assumed its royal title.
connections.note: Southern Lombard principalities survived, and the imperial title represented by the Carolingian-period node followed in 800.

connections.label: Communal autonomy expands
connections.summary: Northern and central Italian communes asserted autonomy against imperial authority, later recognised in the Peace of Constance.
connections.note: The Italian-states entry is a broader regional frame including varied governments; not all gained autonomy together or broke every legal tie with the empire.

connections.label: Communes & southern monarchy coexist
connections.summary: Independent communes, papal lands and the southern Sicilian monarchy formed contrasting centres of power in medieval Italy.
connections.note: This is a contemporary regional relationship, not a claim that northern communes merged to create the Sicilian kingdom or shared one ruler.

connections.label: Naples–Sicily legal union
connections.summary: The Bourbon ruler formally combined the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily as the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.
connections.note: The Sicily timeline entry groups the crowns’ changing history after the 1282 division; their shared monarch did not make them one unchanged state before 1816.

connections.label: Southern annexation & Italian kingdom
connections.summary: Garibaldi’s campaigns and Sardinian intervention brought the Two Sicilies into the new Kingdom of Italy.
connections.note: Unification also involved other states; Venetia joined in 1866 and Rome in 1870, and Italy became a republic in 1946.

connections.label: Christianisation & court connections
connections.summary: Volodymyr’s adoption of Christianity strengthened ecclesiastical and artistic connections between Rus’ and Byzantium.
connections.note: A religious and diplomatic relationship, not incorporation into the Byzantine state or the beginning of all Rus’ settlement.

connections.label: Regional principalities consolidate
connections.summary: Political authority became increasingly dispersed among competing Rus’ principalities.
connections.note: A gradual and overlapping development, not one dated partition into the modern nations of Ukraine, Russia and Belarus.

connections.label: Mongol invasion & tributary power
connections.summary: Mongol conquest, including the sack of Kyiv in 1240, subjected many Rus’ principalities to tribute under the Jochid realm.
connections.note: Rulers, cities and communities survived; not every Rus’ territory experienced identical control, and the Horde was not a renamed Rus’.

connections.label: Moscow expands among principalities
connections.summary: Moscow developed within northeastern Rus’ and expanded amid competition with other principalities under Horde supremacy.
connections.note: One regional path only; Moscow did not inherit every Rus’ land, and the shared medieval history is not exclusive ancestry or a modern territorial entitlement.

connections.label: Western Rus’ lands incorporated
connections.summary: Lithuanian expansion incorporated extensive western and southern Rus’ territories through changing military and dynastic relationships.
connections.note: Ruthenian legal and cultural traditions continued; these lands were not all incorporated at once, and Lithuania did not inherit the whole Kyivan realm.

audit.note: All nodes have at least one sourced relationship. Shared anchors provide onward navigation to other maps; the maps deliberately distinguish cultural frames from political states.
